purpose: Measure D1 directly on the production Deriver B database using isolated temporary tables, without Wallet WASM or local Durable Object storage.
limits: Synthetic four-statement batches on two one-row diagnostic tables do not reproduce the full registration operation or establish Wallet-workload parity.
A read completes before each measured write pair, and write order alternates. The read after each 250 ms timer can include timer-related clock uncertainty.
All batches use fresh first-primary sessions. Native Worker execution colo was not independently captured; targeted placement and trace egress are recorded separately from D1 primary location.
Existing wallet rows were not mutation targets. Only the two task-created diagnostic tables were inserted, updated and dropped. Original table schemas were checked after cleanup.
This probe adds bounded database traffic. It is not a before/after performance comparison or a latency fix.
SQL duration excludes service dispatch and write acknowledgement. Internal D1 timing remains unexposed.
Fast results cannot establish a production-database-specific defect or rule out an intermittent stall.
finding: With identical parameterized UPDATE text and binding shape, 4 of 60 updates changing the stored value took 494–1057 ms. All 60 updates assigning the existing value took 5–10 ms. The long-delay class reproduces on the production B D1 database without Wallet Rust/WASM or wallet-owned Durable Object storage.
controlledDifference: Both update categories use UPDATE <diagnostic_table> SET value = ?1 WHERE id = 1 AND status = admitted, followed by the same three SELECT statements. Only the bound value differs: the existing value or the next sequence value. Order alternates by round.
measured: Reads: median 6 ms, range 5–9 ms, 60 samples.
Existing-value updates: median 7 ms, range 5–10 ms, 60 samples.
Value-changing updates: median 8 ms, range 6–1057 ms, 60 samples. Four exceed 100 ms.
Value-changing SQL execution never exceeded 0.4339 ms. Every statement reports one attempt on the SIN primary.
Both update categories report changed_db=true and one row written.
The original database table schemas match after diagnostic cleanup. Existing wallet rows were not mutation targets.
inferred: The reproduced pause does not require Wallet cryptography, WASM startup, or wallet-owned Durable Object storage.
SQL text and parameter-binding shape do not explain the difference in this control.
The database service path used to complete value-changing writes is the leading location of the pause.
unknown: Internal D1 queueing, storage commit, replication acknowledgement, and response scheduling are not separately exposed.
The experiment does not identify the exact internal mechanism of the original 740 ms admission interval.
No runtime change with a verified latency improvement is established.
reproductionParity: The same production D1 primary reproduces long waits outside SQL execution. Full Wallet admission-workload parity is not established.
